say.text: A 45-year-old man has had years of indigestion and now sudden, severe upper abdominal pain.
Before I teach this, try the problem. Which site do peptic ulcers most often perforate through?

choices.label: Posterior wall of the first part of the duodenum
Anterior wall of the first part of the duodenum
Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: Ask what lies behind each wall. One wall has a major artery behind it.
What happens to a thin wall when an ulcer eats through it?
Yes. The commonest perforation site is the anterior wall of the first part of the duodenum.
Perforation is a full-thickness hole into the free peritoneal cavity, and the anterior wall is where it most often happens.
That is not right. The posterior wall feels like the dangerous one, because it is the wall that bleeds.
Bleeding and perforation are different outcomes. Posterior ulcers erode the gastroduodenal artery and bleed; anterior ulcers are the ones that perforate.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so check the outcome before you pick the wall: bleeding and perforation are not the same event.

say.text: That is not right. Lesser curvature ulcers are the ones most students picture first, so the site feels familiar.
But the question asks which site perforates most often. That is the anterior wall of the first part of the duodenum.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so re-read the question: it asks for the most frequent site, not the most familiar ulcer.

say.text: Two ulcers in the first part of the duodenum. One presents with haematemesis and melaena; the other with sudden peritonitis.
Which pairing of wall and outcome is right, and which artery is eroded in the bleeder?

choices.label: Anterior ulcer bleeds from gastroduodenal artery erosion; posterior ulcer perforates
Posterior ulcer bleeds from left gastric artery erosion; anterior ulcer perforates
Posterior ulcer bleeds from gastroduodenal artery erosion; anterior ulcer perforates
Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: Start with the bleeder. Which artery runs behind the first part of the duodenum, and what does eroding it cause?
That is not right. The deep posterior wall feels like the dangerous one, so it seems the one that would perforate.
But what lies behind each wall decides the outcome. Posterior ulcers erode the gastroduodenal artery and bleed; anterior ulcers perforate into the peritoneal cavity.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so pick the outcome first: a bleed and a perforation come from different walls.

say.text: That is not right. The lesser curvature and its left gastric artery sit close to the stomach, so that artery seems to fit.
The bleeding duodenal ulcer erodes the gastroduodenal artery, not the left gastric artery. The anterior wall is the one that perforates.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so name the artery behind the wall before you accept a neighbouring one.

say.text: Yes. The posterior ulcer bleeds because it erodes the gastroduodenal artery.
The anterior ulcer perforates into the abdomen. The wall tells you the outcome, and the artery behind it tells you the bleed.
A 55-year-old man has sudden abdominal pain. His erect chest X-ray shows free gas under the diaphragm.
What does this picture most often mean?

choices.label: Perforated peptic ulcer is the commonest cause, though others exist
Free gas always means a perforated peptic ulcer, with no other cause
Free gas points to a perforated ulcer until proven otherwise
Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: Look at the qualifier in the question. Is it asking what is always true, or what is most often true?
That is not right. Free gas feels like a sure sign of an ulcer, because perforation is the classic reason for air under the diaphragm.
A perforated peptic ulcer is the most common cause of free intraperitoneal gas. That is a frequency, not a rule, so other causes still exist.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so notice the word 'most' in a frequency statement before you turn it into a rule.

say.text: That is not right. An ulcer is the cause everyone learns first, so it feels like the default reading of free gas.
Perforation is the commonest cause of pneumoperitoneum, a frequency. 'Until proven otherwise' turns that frequency into a rule the claim does not support.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so separate how often a cause occurs from whether it is the only cause.

say.text: Yes. Perforated peptic ulcer is the commonest cause of pneumoperitoneum, so it is the first cause to exclude.
Because it is a frequency, other causes still exist, and the clinical picture decides which one this is.
